flawed_step: The required inference that the marginal laws determine all joint probabilities is unjustified: marginals do not determine the dependence between X and Y.
counterexample: Let X,Y take values in {0,1}. Joint distribution A assigns probability 1/4 to each of (0,0),(0,1),(1,0),(1,1). Joint distribution B assigns probability 1/2 to (0,0), probability 1/2 to (1,1), and probability 0 to (0,1),(1,0). In both A and B, P(X=0)=P(X=1)=P(Y=0)=P(Y=1)=1/2, so both one-dimensional marginals agree. But the joint distributions differ: under A, P(X=Y)=1/2, while under B, P(X=Y)=1.
assessment_summary: The statement is false because identical marginals can be coupled with different dependence structures. The two explicit joint distributions above have exactly the same X- and Y-marginals but are not equal.
